summary: This RFC changes the rules in RFC 2046 about the default charset parameter for text media types, so they match what clients and servers do in practice.

plainLanguage.summary: Old rules said what alphabet to assume when none is stated. Reality did something else, so the rule was changed to match.

questions: what is the default charset for text media types
how does mime charset default work
does text plain default to us-ascii
what did rfc 6657 change in rfc 2046
should new text media types define a default charset
subtitle: Retires the old rule that text media types without a charset parameter are assumed to be US-ASCII.

tldr.problem: RFC 2046 said the default charset for text types was US-ASCII, HTTP used ISO-8859-1 instead, and many clients ignored the rule for types like text/html and text/xml, leaving it unclear which rule was authoritative.
tldr.mechanism: Each text subtype may define its own default charset or none. New registrations SHOULD either not use the charset parameter or require it every time, and protocols MUST NOT override a subtype's default.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6657 updates RFC 2046 and does not change the default of any currently registered media type, so text/plain still defaults to US-ASCII.

facts.label: Suggested default if one is needed

today: RFC 6657 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2012 that updates RFC 2046. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why the Old Default Was Confusing
sections.content:
RFC 2046 specified that the default charset parameter, meaning the value used when the parameter is missing, is US-ASCII. RFC 2616 then changed the default for HTTP to ISO-8859-1. That encoding is not very common for new text/* media types, and the special HTTP rule left it unclear whether RFC 2046 or RFC 2616 was authoritative.

Complex text subtypes such as text/html and text/xml have their own way inside the format to declare the charset, and the RFC notes that many existing user agents ignore the US-ASCII default for at least those two. The goal is to better align the rules with what clients and servers actually do.
sections.plainLanguage: Two rulebooks gave different answers about which alphabet to assume, and many programs ignored both. That made it hard to tell who was right.

sections.title: The New Default Charset Rules
sections.content:
RFC 6657 quotes the old sentence from section 4.1.2 of RFC 2046, which said the default character set assumed without a charset parameter is US-ASCII, and replaces it. Each subtype of text that uses the parameter can define its own default, including having no default.

For interoperability, a text/* registration SHOULD do one of two things: say the charset parameter is not used because the charset travels inside the payload (as in text/xml), or require the parameter to be included unconditionally so no default is needed.

New subtypes SHOULD NOT define a default charset. If there is a strong reason to, they SHOULD use UTF-8. Every new text/* registration MUST clearly specify how the charset is determined, and relying on the RFC 2046 default is no longer permitted.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of text note now decides its own guess, or better, never needs to guess. Anyone creating a new kind must say clearly how to tell the alphabet.

sections.title: Existing Types, text/plain and Protocols
sections.content:
Existing text/* registrations that fail to say how the charset is determined still default to US-ASCII. For text/plain, the default is unchanged from RFC 2046 and remains US-ASCII. The RFC also states that it does not change the defaults for any currently registered media type.

Registrations for types that can carry charset information inside the payload, such as text/html and text/xml, SHOULD NOT specify the charset parameter or any default, to avoid conflicting readings if the parameter and the payload disagree.

The charset rules belong to the subtype, not the protocol. Protocols that use MIME therefore MUST NOT override default charset values for text/* types for their own use, and MUST leave that to the subtype definitions.
sections.plainLanguage: Old kinds of notes keep the guess they already had, and plain text still assumes the basic alphabet. Delivery services are not allowed to change a note type's guess.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC warns that guessing the charset parameter can lead to security issues such as content buffer overflows, denial of service or bypass of filtering mechanisms. This document does not promote guessing and encourages use of charset information specified by the sender.

Conflicting information between in-band and out-of-band sources can cause similar problems. The RFC recommends using the charset information that is more likely to be correct, for example in-band over out-of-band.
sections.plainLanguage: Guessing wrong about the alphabet can let tricky content slip past checks. It is safer to use what the sender actually said.

sections.title: IANA Actions
sections.content:
IANA has updated the text subregistry of the Media Types registry to add a preamble: "See [RFC6657] for information about 'charset' parameter handling for text media types."

IANA has also added RFC 6657 to the list of references at the beginning of the Application for Media Type form, so people registering new types see the new rules.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of note types now points to this RFC, and so does the form people fill in to add a new type.

events.label: RFC 2046 sets US-ASCII as the default charset for text types

RFC 6657 lets each text subtype define its own default, or none
